connection: Session 33 created a working clock-entry endpoint and complete service registration. Invalid requests still lack a deliberate HTTP contract. Add API validation, structured logging, and consistent error responses around the existing endpoint.
objectives: Reproduce the real bug directly: attempt to resolve PayrollService from PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web's real DI container and observe the InvalidOperationException it throws.
Read WebApiRegistrationTests.cs, which already proves this exact failure (and its one-line fix) without needing a running web host.
Apply the real fix: register IEmployeeService/EmployeeService in Program.cs, and confirm PayrollService now resolves successfully.
Connect this fix back to Session 24's throw-vs-return rule: should a missing registration surface as a 500 error, or should the API return a more specific status code?

visuals.title: The real, latent bug
visuals.explanation: PayrollService's constructor requires IEmployeeService; PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/Program.cs registers IClockEntryRepository, IEmployeeRepository, IClockEntryService, and PayrollService itself -- but never IEmployeeService.

visuals.title: Undiscovered because nothing calls it yet
visuals.explanation: Before Session 33 added a controller, and before any controller resolves PayrollService, this bug had no way to surface -- it was real but silent.

visuals.title: The real test proves both the failure and the fix
visuals.explanation: WebApiRegistrationTests.cs's two tests: one confirms resolving PayrollService throws without IEmployeeService registered; the other confirms adding one line fixes it.

visuals.title: A missing DI registration is a different failure than a business rule violation
visuals.explanation: This bug happens before any request-specific logic runs -- Session 24's throw-vs-return rule was about expected domain outcomes, not startup configuration errors like this one.

preQuiz.prompt: Why did the real missing-IEmployeeService-registration bug go undiscovered in the source WebApi project for as long as it did?
options: Nothing in the project ever actually tried to resolve PayrollService -- with zero controllers (confirmed in Session 33), the bug had no code path that would trigger it
It was actually discovered and fixed, then reintroduced
ASP.NET Core silently ignores missing DI registrations
preQuiz.explanation: This is exactly why Session 33's controller work matters here -- once something in the request pipeline resolves PayrollService, the bug becomes immediately, loudly visible.

preQuiz.prompt: What does WebApiRegistrationTests.cs's first test prove, without running a full ASP.NET Core host?
options: That building a ServiceCollection with the real WebApi's exact registrations (minus IEmployeeService) and resolving PayrollService throws InvalidOperationException -- the same failure a real running host would hit
That the real WebApi project fails to compile
preQuiz.explanation: Reproducing a DI container's real registration graph in a fast unit test (no web server needed) is exactly how this bug is demonstrated without the overhead of an integration test.

preQuiz.prompt: What is the one-line fix for this real bug?
options: Add builder.Services.AddSingleton<IEmployeeService, EmployeeService>(); to Program.cs, alongside the other three real registrations already there
Rewrite PayrollService's constructor to not require IEmployeeService
preQuiz.explanation: The fix is additive and minimal -- exactly what WebApiRegistrationTests.cs's second test confirms: adding the missing registration, and nothing else, resolves the failure.

concept.title: Validate at the HTTP boundary
paragraphs: Request validation rejects malformed or incomplete wire data before calling the domain service. Domain invariants still protect the model when callers bypass HTTP.
The two layers answer different questions and should not duplicate every rule.

concept.title: Translate known failures consistently
paragraphs: A known conflict such as clocking in twice should become a deliberate status and error shape. Unexpected exceptions remain server failures and should be logged once at the boundary.
Controllers should not contain duplicated try/catch blocks for every endpoint.

concept.title: Structured logs carry searchable context
paragraphs: Log named values such as EmployeeId and operation outcome rather than building one long string.
Do not log secrets or turn expected validation failures into noisy stack traces.

lab.objective: Add API validation, structured logging, and consistent error responses around the existing endpoint.
lab.startingCondition: Session 33 created a working clock-entry endpoint and complete service registration. Invalid requests still lack a deliberate HTTP contract.

postQuiz.prompt: Why did WebApiRegistrationTests.cs's two tests not need a running ASP.NET Core web server to prove this bug and its fix?
options: The bug is entirely about DI container registration, which a plain ServiceCollection reproduces exactly -- no HTTP request, routing, or web server involvement is needed to trigger or observe it
ASP.NET Core tests always require a running server
The tests are not actually testing the real bug
postQuiz.explanation: Isolating exactly the layer where a bug lives (here, DI registration) is what let this test run fast and without any web-hosting overhead.

postQuiz.prompt: If a second service were added to PayrollService's constructor in the future without updating Program.cs's registrations, what category of bug would result?
options: The same category as this session's real bug -- a missing DI registration, undiscovered until something actually tries to resolve the affected service
No bug -- DI containers automatically register every dependency
postQuiz.explanation: This is exactly why WebApiRegistrationTests.cs's pattern -- reproducing the real registration graph in a fast test -- is worth keeping around: it would catch this exact class of regression immediately.

postQuiz.prompt: Is 'PayrollService cannot be resolved' the same kind of failure as ClockEntryService.Clockout's 'employee not currently clocked in' from Session 24?
options: No -- the first is a startup/configuration failure (a missing registration, unrelated to any specific request's data); the second is an expected, everyday domain outcome Session 24's throw-vs-return rule was written for
Yes -- both should be handled identically
No -- the first cannot actually occur in a real application
postQuiz.explanation: Session 24's rule was scoped to domain-level expected/unexpected outcomes -- this session's bug lives one layer below that, in DI configuration, and is worth naming as a distinct category rather than forcing it into the same rule.

reflections: Why might a bug like this one -- real, verified, and simple to fix -- persist undiscovered in a real project for a long time?
What would you add to this codebase's test suite to catch a similar missing-registration bug the moment a new dependency is introduced, rather than only after this specific one was found?
How does resolving this bug change your confidence in the rest of PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/Program.cs's registrations -- would you want to write a similar test for each one?
whatBreaks: Leaving IEmployeeService unregistered means any future controller action that resolves PayrollService (directly or via a dependency chain) throws InvalidOperationException at the moment of resolution -- a real, silent trap for anyone who adds a new endpoint without knowing this gap exists. Registering EmployeeService with the wrong lifetime (say, Scoped instead of matching the other Singleton registrations) would still fix the immediate resolution failure but introduce the same kind of lifetime-mismatch question Session 30 studied.
summary: PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/Program.cs -- mirroring the real, current the TimeClock Web project/Program.cs -- never registers IEmployeeService, even though PayrollService's constructor requires it; resolving PayrollService throws InvalidOperationException as a result. WebApiRegistrationTests.cs already proves both the failure and its one-line fix without a running web host; this session's lab applies that same fix to the real Program.cs, and distinguishes this startup/configuration failure from Session 24's domain-level throw-vs-return rule.
